title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence & Risk Exceptions
author: Aisha Kapoor
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's authoritative controls and operational procedures for: RBAC & authentication, audit logging and evidence workflows, data residency & retention, secure SDLC requirements, incident response for security events, and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended for platform engineers, security owners, compliance reviewers, and product owners.

Key goals
- Ensure least-privilege access across all environments and automated provisioning via SSO/SCIM.
- Provide tamper-resistant audit trails with defined retention aligned to regulatory and contractual needs.
- Define secure SDLC gates to prevent insecure code/config deploys to production.
- Maintain an executable incident response playbook that preserves evidence for forensic and compliance needs.
- Operationalize compliance evidence collection and a formal risk/exceptions process.

Owners and contacts
- Document owner: Security (Aisha Kapoor)
- Primary on-call (security incidents): security-oncall@redwood.com
- Compliance evidence owner: Compliance Engineering (Elena García)
- RBAC owner: Identity & Access team (Marcus Lee)

1) RBAC and Authentication

Summary
We enforce centralized identity, least privilege roles, and automated provisioning. All access must be authenticated via SSO and protected with MFA.

Platform components and responsibilities
- Identity provider: Okta (SSO + MFA + SCIM provisioning).
- Privileged access: gated by AWS IAM roles for cloud resources and Cortex RBAC for internal admin UIs.
- Secrets and key storage: AWS KMS for hosted, customer-managed KMS/HSM for Private deployments.
- Service accounts: limited to machine principals; no long-lived user credentials.

Standard roles (examples)
- security-admins (full security configuration + audit access)
- infra-operators (deploy/run infra; no customer data access)
- platform-eng (service owner access with scoped escalation)
- customer-support (access to sanitized logs/support tools only)
- read-only (view dashboards and metrics)

Controls and SLOs
- Access reviews: quarterly (every 90 days) automated review by Identity & Access team.
- MFA: required for all human accounts (Okta enforcement).
- Just-in-time elevation: privileged tasks should use ephemeral sessions with approval where possible (JIT via OAuth tokens, valid for <= 8 hours).
- Provisioning SLA: SCIM user provisioning updates must reflect within 5 minutes of change.

2) Audit logging and monitoring

Summary
All security-relevant events are collected centrally and retained according to classification (see Data Residency & Retention). Logs are immutable once ingested and are monitored for anomalies.

Log collection and pipelines
- Sources: application logs, API access logs (edge/API gateway), infrastructure audit logs (AWS CloudTrail), Kubernetes audit, DB audit (where supported), console/admin UI audit.
- Ingestion: Fluentd -> Kafka -> Splunk (long-term) and Datadog (real-time metrics/alerts).
- Tamper-resistance: logs signed at ingestion via HMAC and write-once S3 buckets with object lock for sensitive streams.

SLOs and thresholds
- Ingestion availability: 99.9% (measured per-minute)
- Alerting latency: security-relevant alert must be visible in alerting channel within <= 2 mins of ingestion for high-severity events.
- Retention verification: quarterly integrity checks to verify retention policies and immutability.

3) Data residency and retention

Summary
Data classification drives residency and retention. Customers can select region for Private deployments; hosted API follows region selection controls and contractual agreements.

Classification & retention table (examples)
| Data class | Typical sources | Minimum retention | Retention rationale |
|------------|-----------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Audit logs (security-sensitive) | CloudTrail, admin UI | 7 years | Compliance (SOC2/ISO, contractual) |
| API access logs (usage) | API gateway | 1 year | Billing, forensics |
| Application debug logs | App services | 90 days | Debugging and incident triage |
| Customer PII / regulated data | Customer payloads | Customer-defined / contractual | Data residency and legal compliance |
| Telemetry/metrics | Prometheus/Datadog | 365 days (aggregated) | Performance & capacity planning |

Residency controls
- Hosted: data-at-rest in region selected (US, EU, APAC) using region-specific storage and KMS keys.
- Private: customers run control plane in their VPC; Redwood provides configs to ensure all persisted data remains inside customer-controlled networks.
- Cross-border transfers: blocked by default for regulated data classes; require approval by Legal & Privacy.

4) Secure SDLC (requirements and gates)

Summary
SDLC controls are enforced via automated pipelines, policy-as-code, and mandatory review gates for production changes.

Mandatory gates
1. Static analysis: All PRs must pass SAST (Snyk/CodeQL) with no critical findings.
2. Dependency checks: No high-severity CVEs in direct dependencies; ephemeral exceptions require mitigation plan.
3. Secret scanning: No secrets allowed in repo; failures block PR.
4. Unit & integration tests: Minimum coverage thresholds defined per service (owner-defined).
5. Security review: Changes touching security controls, auth flows, or data handling require Security review label and approval.
6. Canary & rollback: All production deploys must include canary release with automated rollback criteria (latency error > 2x baseline or error rate > 1% sustained over 5 minutes).

Ownership and metrics
- Security PR reviews SLA: Security must respond within 48 business hours for non-urgent changes, 4 hours for high-impact changes.
- Release audit: Each release must publish a release note indicating components, security changes, and evidence links.

5) Incident response: security procedures

Summary
IR procedures combine detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review with evidence preservation to support compliance.

Detection & triage
- Sources: IDS/IPS alerts, SIEM (Splunk) detections, Datadog anomaly alerts, customer reports.
- Triage owner: Security on-call. Classify incident severity (P1–P4).

Immediate containment steps (P1/P2)
1. Isolate impacted hosts (network ACLs / security groups).
2. Preserve artifacts: snapshot relevant volumes (EBS snapshot), export container logs (kubectl logs --all-containers), capture memory if warranted (volatility/FTK).
3. Start an evidence ticket in Jira with chain-of-custody notes.

Forensic preservation examples (commands)
- EBS snapshot: aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-123456 --description "IR snapshot <incident-id>"
- Kubernetes logs: kubectl -n <ns> get pods && kubectl -n <ns> logs <pod> --all-containers > /tmp/<pod>-logs.txt

Communication & escalation
- Incident channel: #sec-incident on Slack (private channel for P1/P2).
- Notifications: Executive summary to Legal and C-level within 2 hours for material incidents.
- External notification: Follow breach notification policy and legal requirements; customer notification SLA depends on severity and contract.

Post-incident
- Postmortem within 7 business days (blameless), action items with owners, and retro incorporated into runbooks.
- Evidence retention: preserve artifacts for minimum of 1 year post-incident or longer if required by legal.

6) Compliance evidence workflows

Summary
To support audits (SOC2, ISO27001, customer audits), we map controls to artifacts, owners, storage location, and retrieval SLAs.

Artifacts and storage
- Source of truth: Compliance Evidence Bucket (restricted GCS/S3) with object-level ACLs and encryption by CMK.
- Typical artifacts: access review exports, SSO logs, change approvals (PR links), system architecture diagrams, runbooks, penetration test reports, vulnerability scan exports.

Evidence request flow (SLA: 5 business days)
1. Request: Create Jira ticket in COMPLIANCE project with required controls and date range.
2. Triage: Compliance Engineer (Elena García) assigns and validates scope within 1 business day.
3. Collection: Owners gather artifacts and push to Compliance Evidence Bucket with metadata.
4. Review: Compliance team validates artifacts against control mapping.
5. Delivery: Provide secure share (restricted link) to requestor and close ticket.

Automation and tooling
- Control mapping lives in a canonical spreadsheet (maintained weekly) and syncs to the compliance dashboard.
- Evidence connectors: automated exports for identity/access logs and CloudTrail are run daily and stored for long-term retention.

7) Risk and exceptions process

Summary
Formal exceptions allow temporary deviations from policy with compensating controls and an expiration. All exceptions are documented and reviewed.

Exception request requirements
- Requestor, affected control(s), technical justification, compensating controls, risk impact, mitigation timeline, proposed expiry date (<= 180 days default).

Review & approval
- Initial review by control owner (3 business days).
- Security Risk Committee approval required for high-impact exceptions (meets weekly).
- Legal/Privacy review mandatory for data residency or cross-border exceptions.

Monitoring and renewal
- Exceptions auto-expire; renewals require re-submission and re-approval.
- Quarterly tracking of active exceptions; high-risk exceptions require monthly status reports.

Appendices
- Links: identity provisioning runbook, logging retention configuration, SDLC checklist, incident-response runbook (internal links).
- Change history: document first published 2024-09-15; major update 2026-02-10 to add evidence automation and extended audit retention requirements.

If you have questions about applying these controls to a specific product or customer deployment, contact the Security team or file a ticket in the Compliance Jira project.
